opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I thought about it early on was pretty simple: biology already has its own language. Proteins are strings of amino acids, DNA is a string of nucleotides, and evolution has been running this enormous experiment for billions of years, writing down what works and throwing away what doesn't. So the question became, if language models can learn grammar, meaning, and even some reasoning just from predicting the next word or a masked word in text, could the same approach learn the rules of biology just from reading sequences?

What made that exciting is that the data was already there. We had hundreds of millions of protein sequences sitting in public databases, and most of them had no labels. Nobody had measured their structure or their function. In traditional machine learning in biology, that's a problem, because you're always bottlenecked on expensive experimental labels. But with self-supervised learning, the unlabeled data becomes the asset. You mask out some amino acids, ask the model to fill them in, and to do that well it has to implicitly learn things like which residues contact each other in 3D, which positions are conserved because they're functionally important, and which mutations are tolerated.

So the agenda was framed around a few core questions. First, does scale help here the way it does in natural language? If you make the models bigger and train on more sequences, do you actually get better biological understanding emerging? Second, can we probe what the model has learned, can we pull structure or function out of its internal representations without ever having trained it on those things directly? And third, can those representations be useful downstream, for predicting the effect of mutations, for predicting structure, and eventually for designing new proteins?

What we found, and what I think surprised a lot of people, is that the answer to those questions was largely yes. Information about structure really does emerge from just sequence modeling. And that shifted my thinking from "language models as a neat trick for biology" to "this might be a foundational way of representing biological knowledge," where the end goal isn't just prediction but actually engineering molecules, moving drug discovery from something that's mostly trial and error toward something that looks a lot more like design.

r001.rationale: The response frames the agenda as asking whether language models could learn biology’s rules by learning from protein and DNA sequences, analogously to learning language from text.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the framing really came out of a pretty simple observation. If you look at a protein sequence, it's a string of characters, twenty amino acids, and evolution has been writing these strings for billions of years. Every protein that exists today is one that worked well enough to survive, and that means the statistics of those sequences encode an enormous amount of information about structure and function. So the question we asked was: if you train a language model on hundreds of millions of these sequences, with no labels, just the raw text of biology, what does it learn?

And the bet was that it would learn something deep, the same way GPT-style models trained on next-token prediction end up learning syntax and semantics and world knowledge without anyone telling them to. In biology, the equivalent of grammar is biophysics. A residue that's buried in the core of a protein has to be hydrophobic. Two residues that are in contact have to co-vary over evolution so the structure is preserved. The model has to pick up on those constraints to predict the masked amino acid well.

So the agenda had a few pieces. First, scale. We wanted to see whether the scaling behavior that people saw in natural language would show up in proteins, and it did. As we went from millions to billions of parameters, the models got better at things we never explicitly trained them for, like predicting contact maps or the effect of a mutation. Second, we wanted to work directly from the single sequence, not from a multiple sequence alignment, because that unlocks proteins that don't have a lot of evolutionary neighbors, and it makes everything much faster. And third, the long-term vision was generation. If the model understands the language, it should be able to write in it. You should be able to prompt it with a function or a structure and have it design a new protein that nature never produced.

I think the honest thing to say is that we didn't have perfect foresight. We started with representation learning and the structure prediction and design pieces emerged as the models got good enough to make them possible. But the core framing never changed: treat biology as a language, trust that scale and self-supervision will extract the underlying rules, and then see how far that takes you.

r001.rationale: The response frames protein sequences as language and compares their learning to GPT-style models learning human-language structure. It does not mention DNA sequences, so it does not communicate the complete criterion.

astra-6.text:
The way I framed it was: language models learn patterns from sequences, and biology has a lot of information encoded in sequences. Could we use that same approach to learn something useful about proteins—how their sequence relates to their structure and function?

The important question was what that would let us do. Predicting properties is useful, but could we go further and design a protein with a particular function? That gives you a research agenda that connects modeling to experiments: build a model, use it to propose something, test it, and learn from where the predictions break down.

r001.rationale: The response compares applying language models’ sequence-learning approach to proteins, but it does not mention DNA or clearly frame the analogy as learning biological sequences like human language.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I framed it was: can we learn the language of biology in a way that lets us design new things? In human language, you train on sequences of words. In biology, proteins are sequences of amino acids, and those sequences encode information about structure and function. So there’s a natural question of how much of that information a model can learn directly from sequence.

But learning patterns is only the first step. The more interesting question is whether you can use those patterns to design a protein with a property you care about. That makes experimental validation central to the research agenda: generate a hypothesis, test it in the lab, and use what you learn to improve the next design. The goal is to connect better models to better biological experiments.

r001.rationale: The response compares learning human word sequences with learning protein amino acid sequences, but it does not mention DNA sequences, so it does not communicate the full criterion.
